The Mermaid's Tongue might be an alluring prospect, but choosing to use it displays a dangerous hubris.

Dirk was modelled after popular movie actors you might have seen in blockbusters in the 2010s.

He's got skinny legs because he's not a body builder - his muscle is mostly just for aesthetics.

I gave him simple dot eyes to make him seem naive and somewhat clueless.

-Adam

Dirk is the most contemporary character in the Grimoire universe - he even wears jeans and sunglasses.

I first referenced to old-timey poster boy movie stars, but final design is inspired by more modern celebrities. Like the majority of male movie stars, we wanted him to have a generic superhero build.

-Catherine

Adam and I drew character concepts separately and then we would compare and develop the characters further based on a combination of the ideas.

I originally drew Dirk with blue puppydog eyes, but Adam drew Dirk with naive-looking dot eyes which felt more in line with his character, so it stuck.

-Catherine

In case you're thinking it: yes, I was consciously evoking Johnny Bravo with the animation smears.

Dirk was very fun to pose, and some of these sketches became animation poses with almost no revisions. Dirk draws from a rich lineage of Good Boys.

-Velvet

Gripp’s original inspiration was somewhere between an eccentric snake oil salesman and Willy Wonka.

I liked the idea that his face could be wide-eyed and overly friendly - and then quickly become dark and scheming.

-Catherine

Eventually I started to incorporate the aeronautical theme into his look.

I experimented with compass belt buckles, propeller bow ties, and eventually the recognisable hot air balloon hat.

Once we shrunk down a version of this hat for Cornelius Cane to wear, we knew we had found our Gripp.

-Catherine

Gripp was surprisingly hard to animate. We simplified him quite a bit after I came on, but he still has a lot going on and very difficult proportions to control. I love how he turned out though.


I'm pretty sure he has the most unique poses of any Grimoire character ever, too. I hope you appreciate them!

-Velvet

Here, Catherine arrives at the final design for the Mortuga Submarine.

One of the last major changes we made was to the scope of the wooden sailing ship - the Dearest Selena. We realised it needed to be much smaller and simpler (with only one sail, rather than several) as it could apparently be crewed by only two people.

-Adam

I imagined Mariana as a wandering countryside historian - an old-fashioned dapper look, but messy and mud-scuffed from her time crawling around the brambles.

Really, the only thing from this drawing that we kept was the fact that she has a pipe.

-Adam

Mariana Moon's keywords were nomadic historian, professor and hobbit.

Naturally, tweed jackets, waistcoats and a tobacco pipe seemed like a fitting combination.

She's also an older character, and I struggled with capturing her age at first.

-Catherine

Since she was a nomad, I imagined she needed to carry all of her worldly possessions wherever she went. In one image, I drew her wearing all her clothes at once.

I also started drawing her with moon-shaped accessories, which eventually made it into her final design.

-Catherine

Bilbo Baggins was referenced a fair bit in discussions of Mariana's mannerisms. (Marianarisms?) This came across especially in the bottom-middle drawing, which made it into animation with only a little alteration.


I like to imagine she always knows a little bit more than she's letting on, and isn't above teasing you with that fact.

-Velvet

There were rumours that Mortuga was under a curse and couldn’t leave the submarine to see the light of day, much like a vampire.

He is visual combination of Sinbad, Captain Nemo and Count Dracula. I gave him sunken vampiric features, as we wanted him to seem intimidating.

-Catherine

I tried to imagine the way this curse might effect his appearance - his hair starting to look like coral.

We also needed to show off an important scar on his arm, so I came up with the idea of him wearing half a ripped jacket.

-Catherine

I remember seeing fishing boats on a trip to Vietnam that had eyes painted on the front of every boat. One of the reasons for this was to scare away sea monsters.

I loved this idea and added a similar feature to the back of the submarine.

-Catherine

One of the last major changes we made was to the scope of the wooden sailing ship - the Dearest Selena. We realised it needed to be much smaller and simpler (with only one sail, rather than several) as it could apparently be crewed by only two people.

-Adam

There are several clues in the game that show what the extended Fellow family looked like, so it was important that we spent some time drawing them.

Designing them together meant that I was able to balance their likeness to one another and consciously make them look related.

-Catherine

Some cleaned up art to confirm the final designs for several side characters, including their 'meeples' for the model town.

From top left: Baroness Fortuna, Governor Fellow, Selena Stonetop, Damian Dusk, Felicia Stonetop.

-Adam

As a retired circus performer, her unique appearance feels like an old stage costume.

I drew clothes that were a cross between swimsuit and costume, even giving her theatrical faux lashes and stage make-up.

She salvages items from the sea to decorate her room, so I loved the idea of her wearing pirate treasure as jewellery.

When Sinthia was first conceived, her name was Dorothy Drummond. She was less of an intrepid mechanic and more of a goody-two-shoes genius who always knew the right answer - her hair evoking someone eagerly raising their hand in a classroom.

This particular outfit was inspired by German mathematician Emmy Noether.

-Adam

The first character I drew in the game, an experienced young mechanic turned newbie submarine captain.

I enjoyed playing around with the idea that she would wear nuts, bolts and spanners in her hair and as jewellery.

At one point I gave her an oversized spanner - which felt a little too fantastical. 

-Catherine

I wanted Sinthia's appearance to suggest that her new captain’s role was ill-fitted for her.

I put her in an oversized authoritative sea captain’s jacket, that is clumsily worn over her mechanic's overalls like an afterthought.

-Catherine

In tweaking Sinthia's design for animation we removed the big collar on her coat: it just distracted from her face and hurt the silhouette.


Her movement is relatively understated, but I feel she has a great range from faux-confident captain to cheeky young girl to nervous teen. She's dealing with a lot and trying hard to mask her stress, so it's fitting.

-Velvet

Symmetry was originally called Felicity Fog. Eventually, we realised we shouldn't have a Felicity and a Felicia, so I came up with Symmetry Silkmoth instead.

Sym's crystal ball being known as the 'Fog Ball' is a vestigial trace of her original name.

-Adam

Sym was originally considered the prime suspect and to add to the suspicion, we wanted her to be spooky looking - pale features, white victorian clothes, a body shaped like a ghost and a face like vacant doll.

I added an eye on her locket, a symbol that became synonymous with her mentor, Zephyr.

-Catherine

She's an illusionist-in-training, so I perched a tiny wizard hat on her head, gave her magicians gloves and a cape that was far too big for her.

There was also a phase where I imagined the eye on her locket would always look in the same direction she was looking. One of her tricks!

-Catherine

Sym is one of those characters where translating Adam's design into three dimensions was a lot of fun. She has a great box-shaped head so it was important to me that it work from all angles.


I ended up giving her some subtle rubber-hose arms in motion, making her look a bit more pathetic and adding to her antiquated image by evoking 1930s animation.

-Velvet

Tadpole was a very difficult character to design! We had to change her head shape several times before we finally landed on something we were happy with.

In the name of simplifying the design, we also removed some of the extra details I initially wanted - like shark bite marks on her arms.

-Adam

Madam Tadpole is a peculiar character, as you're not sure if she is human or a fish.

At one point I really leant into that idea of her being a human fish and drew her with fish style features, put barnacles on her body and gave her hair made of seaweed that she styled to look like a fin.

-Catherine

As a retired circus performer, her unique appearance feels like an old stage costume.

I drew clothes that were a cross between swimsuit and costume, even giving her theatrical faux lashes and stage make-up.

She salvages items from the sea to decorate her room, so I loved the idea of her wearing pirate treasure as jewellery.

-Catherine

Tadpole's body language is usually understated, even graceful, but occasionally she'll break out into a broad motion that makes use of her huge arms in a way that's quite striking.

I wanted to give her shark teeth at first, but it ended up being too distracting.

-Velvet

This is my earliest drawing of Wirman. I imagined him with a perpetual five o'clock shadow, wrinkled clothes and a dated haircut.

I always felt like he should look like he belongs in the 1970s.

-Adam

A writer who’s a little rough around the edges and seemingly always grumpy.

Adam was keen on referencing Stephen King for this character - which is where his furrowed brow and pained expression were derived from.

-Catherine

At one point my version of Wirman started to look a little too confident.

I remedied this by make his hair look less styled, giving him loose clothing and a hunched posture - a bad habit acquired from hours writing away on his typewriter.

-Catherine

To me Wirman is the Professor Pointer of this game, in that he feels very similar to myself.


Adam reduced his chin after I did these sketches as it didn't feel right for him to have such a strong jaw. This results in quite a squidgy, nuanced head shape that makes for very fun facial expressions. It also means you can draw him a bit wrong and it'll still look like him.

-Velvet

This was my first drawing of Zephyr. I always imagined him draped in long, old-fashioned scholar's robes.

-Adam

Zephyr’s odd profession as a Dream Doctor was the leading point of my original sketches. I wanted him to look wise, but equally spiritual and eccentric.

The tattooed eye on his head was to suggest a third all-seeing eye. Adding the spectacles was a turning point for me, because it made him look slightly dissociated and somewhat sinister.

-Catherine

His outfit is inspired by wise men from the ages such as Charles Darwin and Isaac Newton, but this opulent style also ties into his image as an avid collector of strange antiquities.

I thought it would be fun to make his hand a literal antique.

-Catherine

Zephyr is one of the hardest characters I've ever had to animate!

He has everything: tall so his proportions are difficult to control, moves slowly so needs lots of drawings, flowing fabric so tons of secondary motion to manage. I'm extremely proud of how he turned out though.

-Velvet

The benefit of a submarine made of two former vessels means some areas work as a time capsule, giving you window into the past - great for environmental storytelling.

Something big and violent happened on the Dearest Selena ship and we used the blood-red sky to add to that uneasy feeling.

-Catherine

A submarine that is part metal and part wooden ship is a bit too fantastical to be believable.

To remedy this, I imagined the wooden parts acting like a skin over a metal interior; eroded, decaying and peeling away from being underwater too long.

-Catherine

This is an important story location, but players aren't given much to do other than to collect the Figurehead clue.

Originally, your discoveries here prompted a discussion between Grimoire and Sally, but several of those were cut from the scope, as I generally found it more interesting to save all those revelations and conclusions for the ending.

-Adam

After travelling for much of her life, Madam Tadpole wants to settle down. Despite it being an airlock, she's made the room feel homely.

The decorations were salvaged from the sea, so everything is slightly broken or tarnished. The images on the wall were from a shipwreck, photographs of long lost souls.

-Catherine

I wanted this room to create the illusion that you are underwater, so I added elements like a coral reef 'shelf', a light feature that looks like suspended jellyfish, and pillows that look like sea anemones.

It's a bright, pastel-coloured respite from the rest of the game, which is often gloomy.

-Catherine

It's interesting how ocean-themed colour palettes can be the obvious dark greens and blues, but they can also be the soft, light pastels of seashells and pearls.

-Adam

This environment is a bit of an outlier, as it's fully dark when you first try to explore it. Despite this, there was a surprising amount of thought put into designing it - as it hides many secrets.

At one point I made the water pumps look like creepy faces that emerge from the darkness as players explored the room by torchlight.

-Catherine

Using the Cell Phone's flashlight to illuminate this room is the most 'Adventure Game Item Puzzle' moment we've ever had in a Detective Grimoire game - normally we try to stray away from that kind of thing.

It provided a fun back-and-forth between Grimoire and Sally, though.

-Adam

Eventually, the vent is opened and the room is partially illuminated from above.

This ends up having a fairly important mechanical function in the story.

-Adam

A secret room in the Dream Chamber, packed with even more with curious items.

Since the shelves of items were the focus of this location, I couldn’t get away with drawing vague objects like I did in the Dream Chamber. I spent some time researching and thinking of what those items could be.

-Catherine

Much like the Dream Chamber, I had to balance the artwork so that some objects felt less important than others.

My trick for this is to colour unimportant objects closer to the background, use dark gradients to hide some away, and if possible - add lighting to draw your eye to the objects of importance.

-Catherine

This room is full of things that have the potential to be clue objects - but by this point in the game, Grimoire and Sally have plenty of clues and they're becoming rather blasé about seeing yet more treasure chests and crystal balls.

The exception, of course, being the thing in the central cabinet.

-Adam

This room was Mortuga’s space, so it needed to feel like it was missing something - the empty chair staring right at you felt appropriate.

The area is covered in old rags and cobwebs, untouched and forgotten.

-Catherine

We later added the Iron Bell to the room which loomed over the captain's desk in an almost metaphorical way.

The wood carvings on the wall also act as a metaphor - a huge, open-mouthed creature, almost engulfing the Captain into the sea.

-Catherine

I wonder if people who have recently played Tangle Tower were stopped in their tracks when they saw that empty birdcage hanging from the ceiling...

-Adam

Unused since Mortuga's death, this secret room feels slightly haunted. There are blown out candles and a eerie blue glow coming from a single tiny window that makes the area feel more private.

Eventually, I framed the room with a tight corridor to make players feel like they were peering into something they were not meant to see.

-Catherine

There are a few moments where light plays a key role in this little room, and the mood changes several times throughout the game depending on what part of the story you're experiencing.

-Catherine

Originally, the Film Projector was found in the Model Town's lighthouse - projecting onto the curtain drawn across the door.

I still prefer it this way around, but sometimes you have to make undesirable compromises for logistical reasons.

-Adam

Mariana Moon has created a cosy campsite nestled amongst the cargo crates in the belly of the ship.

She covered the ground in coal and twigs to replicate the feeling of being outside on a forest floor.

-Catherine

No campsite is complete without a campfire, but of course the logistics of having one on the floor of a submarine (that is partly made of wood) is not a good idea.

As a substitute I used an industrial-style cast iron furnace as a more believable alternative; emanating light, heat and sparks.

-Catherine

Observant players will have noticed that this room originally belonged to the Dearest Selena, not the Seafoam Submarine.

Makes you wonder what's in all those storage crates.

-Adam

This bedroom was intended for a young Sinthia and has remained unchanged for years.

Due to the damp nature of the submarine, the wallpaper is peeling away, making the room seem old and haunted. All the toys and decor are sea-themed, including a 'rocking seahorse' and a 'doll’s submarine'.

-Catherine

Sym is an illusionist by trade, so we imagined her practising her tricks in here.

There is a freestanding walking stick to sell the idea and I also used a fallen lamp to create an eerie stage-like feel to the room.

Her suitcase was aptly inspired by 20th century magician travelling cases.

-Catherine

The Seafoam Submarine was conceived when Sinthia was quite young, so this room was to be her playroom, possibly her bedroom. However, it never ended up being used for that purpose.

The 'painting' at the back was used to provide an immediate example of Sym's illusionist trickery, before she's properly revealed to the player.

-Adam

We wanted the Control Room to feel a bit like a superhero’s lair.

We were keen to avoid the submarine looking too overtly steampunk (to avoid it looking too much like Captain Nemo’s Nautilus) but in this case we allowed ourselves to lean into the aesthetic a little.

-Catherine

This room had a few dependencies, which meant it took a while to finish. The Control Panel and the Captain’s Jacket needed to be defined before they were drawn into the image.

The submarine design itself also needed to be finalised so we knew what shape the viewing deck window would be.

-Catherine

The end result is a realy impressive example of adventure game background design - particularly in terms of fitting a whole bunch of stuff onto the screen.

You could originally look through the periscope, but I took it out when I was searching for things to cut from the game's scope.

-Adam

This room was one of the rare moments where I made a 3D model to help Catherine with the illustration.

Something about the perspective of that little staircase was just really difficult to visualise without blocking it out in 3D.

-Adam

There are two bunk rooms in the game and we needed them to feel distinct from each other.

In this case we wanted the room to mirror the roommate’s personalities. Wirman's side is shoved in a corner, badly presented and messy. He’s too consumed with writing his book to keep things tidy.

-Catherine

In stark contrast is Dirk’s neat, tidy and expensive side of the room.

His bunk looms over Wirman’s like he’s on a pedestal, whilst Wirman works away behind the scenes.

Adam found the hanging tuxedo humorous, because why would you ever need one in a submarine. Celebrities always need a tux right?

-Catherine

This room has some of my favourite Grimoire and Sally examine dialogue.

If you missed them, next time try clicking on the punching bag, the dumbbell, or the pile of books.

I also love the way Amber (as Sally) says 'you never know when you might have to go to a fancy party' in response to the tuxedo.

-Adam

To sell this room as a functioning airlock we needed to add practical features like a door, a water pump and a ladder to get in and out.

In the final artwork, the ladder leans back and becomes horizontal at one point. We decided to not change it, despite it not making much sense. Call it artistic licence. 

-Catherine

The secondary purpose of this space was as a hiding place for Tadpole’s valuables.

We wanted the room to look like the familiar image of sunken treasure at the bottom of the ocean.

This classic, predictable image of ocean treasure was a good way to hide something very important in plain sight.

-Catherine

For a long time, this room was called 'The Ocean's Eye' - because it looks out into the ocean, and because I wanted rooms with cool, memorable names.

When I realised I had never established that it had any kind of name at all, I sheepishly changed it to the rather more mundane 'Dome Tank'.

-Adam

This room took a long time to draw as it needed to be densely packed with trinkets, oddities and posters - to reflect Zephyr's eccentric obsession for collecting curios.

The level of detail meant I needed to carefully use composition and colour to make sure the clues and puzzles stood out.

-Catherine

This room is a combination of a victorian operating theatre, a gothic science lab and a curiosity shop.

The stained glass ceiling was inspired by a dream catcher, with the idea that even the room itself would have its dreams captured.

-Catherine

To me, this room is somewhat reminiscent of Remington's office from Secret of the Swamp, and Fifi's library from Tangle Tower.

Grimoire and Sally always seem to find themselves in places like this.

-Adam

We liked the idea that Gripp’s shop would look like he set it up straight out of the balloon’s crash site, tangled up in the pipes with his basket still swinging mid-air.

The logo on the balloon itself conveniently acts as a huge sign looming over the shop.

-Catherine

Gripp has used the engine room in inventive ways. The compasses are displayed on spinning cogs that rotate them like shop items in a video game.

A big star painted on the giant rotating cog in the background making the shop look like a 'special offer' advert. He’s even created his own customers out of cardboard.

-Catherine

I have to assume Gripp sleeps curled up in his basket at night, because I'm not seeing any evidence to the contrary.

Several people in this game don't have obvious beds or bedrooms. We had a similar problem with Tangle Tower.

-Adam

This is the first time you set foot on the Mortuga submarine and we wanted it to feel unwelcoming and foreboding.

The buoy’s chain leads the player’s eye towards a dark, uninviting open door.

The puddles of water were a good opportunity for creepy reflections.

-Catherine

Originally the Seafoam name was crossed out with red paint, but Adam and I agreed it was too cliché for a murder mystery. The yellow does a good job at feeling aggressive without being too macabre.

-Catherine

(Plus the yellow paint will help confused players find the doorway!
-Adam)

Originally I'd planned a 'Harbor' area between the Town Square and the Fore Deck, where you'd fully see the submarine sitting in the water.

Catherine convinced me that we didn't need it. She was right!

-Adam

The most important location in the game - the crime scene.

Adam already had a clear vision for this space and created a 3D mock-up.

Along with the cauldron, he was keen on the porthole also being in the centre of the room like it was watching - almost like the sea itself was a witness to the murder.

-Catherine

It was here we decided, for dramatic effect, that the cauldron would emanate an eerie, otherworldly, green light.

This green light is a recurring theme throughout the game and we wanted it to feature heavily here.

-Catherine

The Illusion Theatre takes the form of a locked room with no way for anyone to witness the crime.

Unless of course, they were out in the ocean, looking in through the window...

-Adam

This is a 3D model I made to explain my vision to Catherine.

It was a particular combination of ideas; the dead end of a utilitarian submarine corridor, the world's smallest magic show, and a window looking out into the mysterious void of the ocean.

-Adam

One of the few communal areas of the submarine, we wanted this room to feel like a cosy old tavern.

The industrial aesthetic and shape of this submarine room made it a fun challenge. Coral is hanging from the ceiling, as we always try and bring ocean imagery into the submarine wherever possible.

-Catherine

The original submarine’s purpose was to ferry the Silkwirm Sea Serpent, so I experimented with the visual of the serpent, which might have been used as a decorative theme.

I imagined that the current crew would have built the Mess Hall on top of this dramatic feature, hanging kitchen pots from it and building shelves onto it.

-Catherine

A big central room where all the characters can gather at once is something we didn't really have in Tangle Tower.

In this game we've got two of them! - and the characters do actually gather in both of them!

-Adam

Catherine drew this layout image for the crowd scene in the Mess Hall.

I love how the composition fits in all the different characters - it feels like a Renaissance painting.

-Adam

After seeing the Fore Deck, we wanted surprise players here by creating an opulent mansion style room that would contrast to the submarine’s cold metallic exterior.

Ornate paintings decorate the curved walls, including a huge ominous Mermaid painting setting up the themes of the game.

-Catherine

I tried to concept a fireplace that you could believably find aboard a submarine, and it started to look more like some sort of furnace.

Despite there being a fire in the middle of the room, we didn’t want the space to feel too cosy, so we opted for the pink-coloured flame to keep the room feeling unfamiliar.

-Catherine

Most submarines don't have an opulent parlor, so we might have to admit this was somewhat influenced by the Nautilus from Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea.

It also functions very nicely as the kind of room in which the suspects might eventually gather to be accused by a detective...

-Adam

Catherine also drew this layout for the late-game crowd scene in the Parlor.

It's always fun seeing all the suspects in the same room together.

-Adam

The first scene in the game. The original idea was to have players think they might already be on board a ship, so the space is very wooden for this reason.

The abandoned inn has wooden slats on the windows, which we used to create dramatic lighting when the green light of the submarine appears.

-Catherine

Here we wanted to seed the idea of the themes of Silkwirm-on-sea by showing a lot of sea serpent imagery.

-Catherine

I liked the idea of starting the game in a seemingly inconsequential location, but have it gain meaning as you play through the story.

Although, for people who have played Tangle Tower, the 'Stonetop' name may ring a bell immediately.

-Adam

One of my big tasks was the design the Mortuga Submarine itself.

It's a cross between an old sailing ship and a metal submarine. It also needed to believably house most of the locations within the game.

The front of the submarine needed a large viewing deck which would later inform the look of the Control Room.

-Catherine
Submarine 3D Model

During my research, I found an image of a submarine that looked like a shark, which inspired me to characterise the submarine with a face - like it was a sea creature.

At one point I collaged together various fish images to try and create interesting silhouettes that felt familiar but also alien.

-Catherine

I remember seeing fishing boats on a trip to Vietnam that had eyes painted on the front of every boat. One of the reasons for this was to scare away sea monsters.

I loved this idea and added a similar feature to the back of the submarine.

-Catherine

Here, Catherine arrives at the final design for the Mortuga Submarine.

One of the last major changes we made was to the scope of the wooden sailing ship - the Dearest Selena. We realised it needed to be much smaller and simpler (with only one sail, rather than several) as it could apparently be crewed by only two people.

-Adam
Submarine Design

I used the rudimentary modelling skills I'd learned from making Crow Country to make this basic reference model for the shape of the Mortuga Submarine.

Catherine then used this reference model to make paint-overs from a few different angles, in order to give Kindra more information about the colours, patterns and textures.

-Adam

This was one of my favorite and final major pieces to have worked on, especially given the challenge of having to “smash” together multiple different types of ships, styles, and materials into one cohesive whole.

It was quite an interesting puzzle to solve!

-Kindra

The composition and texture of this piece was really rewarding to work on!

It was so exciting to see some of the previous clues I had worked on either refer to - or literally be a part of - this piece.

-Kindra

The second bunk room in the submarine, but instead of being split like Dirk and Wirman's room, it’s a harmonious meeting of two very good friends.

Sym and Sinthia have a shared longing for daylight and have tried to replicate this by sticking yellow paper over the porthole to simulate the sun.

-Catherine

We wanted the room to look like a postcard-perfect countryside scene. They’ve used pots and pans to decorate the room with various plants.

The idyllic miniature house in the centre of the room used to belong to Sym and Sinthia’s pet, Tremblemouse, who didn’t make it into the final game.

-Catherine

Bedrooms are a great way to show how a character is feeling, and this room was used to show Sym and Sinthia's yearning to live amongst sunlight and nature.

Even when the pet mouse was removed from the game, we kept the  little wooden house as it importantly represented the kind of home Sym and Sinthia wanted to have.

-Adam

The biggest story in this abandoned fishing town is the discovery of a sea serpent, which we represented with a statue in the town square.

It felt more impactful to show a close up of the fisherman’s foot holding down the serpent, driving home the narrative of the serpent being the town’s conquest.

-Catherine

Silkwirm-on-sea is named after the silkworm, the larva of a silkmoth, which carry symbolism of transformation and death.

I was drawn to the concept of the silkworm as the mortal shell that perishes and the silkmoth as the ethereal ghost that transcends.

-Adam

The idea I had in my head was that Silkwirm-on-sea was a town that was dead.

Laying at its feet was the monolith of the submarine - acting as the town's grave, with its departed denizens buried within.

You can tell what kind of mood I was in when I was coming up with this stuff, huh.

-Adam

Some of these buildings are an early insight into the suspects you have yet to meet, so it felt important to design them properly.

I created concept art for the whole high street, even the shop branding. One of these designs was the emblem for the Stonetop family, which would appear on the inn and in several other places throughout the game.

-Catherine
